children: Iron ore prices fell on Wednesday after a four-session winning streak, weighed down by concerns over demand in top consumer China as some steelmakers cut output amid shrinking margins, while higher ore imports also added pressure.
The most-traded iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
was down 0.61% at 735.5 yuan ($109.63) a metric ton, as of 0159 GMT. It hit a six-week high at 745 yuan on Tuesday.
The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange slid 1.16% to $99.85 a ton by 0149 GMT after touching a 12-week high the day before.

Four construction steel producers in southwestern China's Sichuan province planned to trim output by as much as 680,000 tons between September and December to balance supply and demand, analysts at consultancy Mysteel said in a note on Tuesday.
The planned reductions are limited, but the move added to concern that weak demand and thinner profit margins could force more mills to curb production, reducing appetite for iron ore.
Pressuring ore prices were also higher-than-expected imports in August as multiple typhoons delayed customs clearance in July.

"A supply glut would keep ore prices under pressure in the medium term despite a recent rebound partly aided by anticipation of a flurry of pre-holiday restocking," analysts at broker First Futures said in a note.
China's state iron ore buyer has asked some domestic steelmakers to hold off buying Rio Tinto
iron ore, as supply contract talks with the world's largest iron ore supplier are underway, Reuters reported, citing three sources.
The new directive is not a procurement ban, the sources said, raising speculation among some traders that a deal between the two sides is close.
